S02.text: By the end, you'll know how often history let the roll beat double, when it fell short, and roughly where the line sits that your own twenty years would have to clear. First, the bond. It's a Series EE savings bond, sold by the U.S. Treasury itself. For bonds issued May to October twenty twenty-six, it earns a fixed two point four zero percent a year, and the rate for new bonds is reset every May and November. That rate alone would not double the money in twenty years, so at the twenty-year mark the Treasury tops the bond up to at least double. The promise, as written, covers bonds held electronically, which is how the Treasury sells them now. Spread over those twenty years, that doubling can also be written as one steady yearly rate, shown here on the gate. And the double only arrives at twenty years: a bond cashed earlier earns just its fixed rate, and one cashed before five years also gives up three months of interest.

S03.text: The Treasury bill path works the other way around: it makes no promise past three months. A bill is a short loan to the government: the buyer pays a bit less than the face amount and gets the full amount back when it comes due. Over twenty years the money rolls through eighty bills, each paying whatever rate the market sets at the time. In August twenty twenty-six, the three-month bill paid three point seven two percent. [thoughtful] It's tempting to set that next to the bond's doubling rate and call it settled. But these rates aren't measured the same way, and bill rates are quoted on a scale where the doubling line sits a little lower. The bigger problem is time: that rate covers one bill, and the roll lives on eighty of them. What decides the race is the bill rate across all twenty years, and that is exactly what nobody knows in advance, us included. So instead of guessing, we went back and replayed history.
